name: Knudson's Two-Hit Hypothesis
statement: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis holds that cancer arises from a tumor suppressor gene only after both of its alleles have been inactivated by separate mutational hits.
statementAccent: both of its alleles have been inactivated
meaning: The hypothesis holds that both copies of a tumor-suppressor gene must be inactivated, by mutation or epigenetic silencing, before its protective function is lost. In inherited cancer syndromes one defective allele is present from birth, so a single additional somatic hit suffices. In sporadic cases both hits must occur independently in the same cell.
mechanism: In hereditary cases a child inherits one already-mutated allele in every cell (the first hit), so only one additional somatic mutation is needed to inactivate the second allele and trigger a tumour, allowing earlier and multifocal disease. In sporadic cases both inactivating mutations must occur by chance in the same somatic cell, which is statistically rarer and later in onset, typically producing a single unilateral tumour.

examples.text: Knudson’s 1971 statistical analysis of retinoblastoma age-of-onset and laterality in familial versus sporadic cases provided the original evidence for the two-hit model, later confirmed molecularly for the RB1 gene.
The hypothesis led to the identification of tumour suppressor genes as a class, and Alfred Knudson received the 1998 Albert Lasker Clinical Medical Research Award for this work.

The related concept of field cancerisation, in which multiple primary tumours arise in one region, is consistent with an initial hit predisposing an entire tissue field before second hits occur locally.

whyItMatters: The two-hit hypothesis established the concept of tumour suppressor genes and recessive-acting cancer genes, reshaping cancer genetics and explaining hereditary predisposition to specific cancers. It remains foundational to modern understanding of oncogenesis and genetic cancer-risk counselling.
limits: The model applies most cleanly to classic tumour suppressors such as RB1 and does not fit genes exhibiting haploinsufficiency, where loss of just one allele already promotes malignancy. Some cancers arise through alternative mechanisms, such as chromothripsis, a catastrophic single-event chromosomal shattering rather than sequential hits.
misreadings: It is sometimes oversimplified as claiming exactly two mutations cause all cancers, when the model specifically concerns the two-allele inactivation of a given tumour suppressor gene, not the total mutational burden of a tumour.
origin: Proposed by Alfred G. Knudson in 1971 through a statistical analysis of retinoblastoma published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
